title: 用智能体构建雄心勃勃的软件：Dioxus 的基础设施与质量实践
author: AI Engineer
content:
Brief Description

Jonathan Kelley reflects on building Dioxus, an ambitious Rust-based cross-platform application framework, and on what changed when coding agents became capable enough to contribute to serious systems work. He argues that AI can accelerate implementation, debugging, documentation, releases, and test infrastructure, but that ambitious software still depends on maintainable foundations, deliberate architecture, careful review, and a high quality bar.

Table of Contents

  • Building Dioxus from an ambitious premise
  • What five years of infrastructure work produced
  • Adopting coding agents without becoming a slop cannon
  • The quality substrate of ambitious software
  • Where agents make hard work tractable
  • Using agents for maintenance and release discipline
  • The limits of AI-written tests and the importance of architecture
  • Code is cheap; quality is not

Building Dioxus from an ambitious premise

Five years ago, Jonathan Kelley made the first commit to a project called Dioxus. During his last undergraduate summer, instead of taking an internship at Google or pursuing AI research like many of his friends, he explored an idea for a cross-platform application framework written in Rust.

In 2021, Rust was still relatively niche, though its ecosystem and tooling were improving. Native performance, a solid type system, and straightforward cross-compilation appealed to him. The idea behind Dioxus was simple: rather than moving among many toolchains, languages, and IDEs, developers could write applications in Rust while using HTML and CSS for markup.

At the time, React Native was unreliable, Flutter was too slow for some needs, and neither performed well with native APIs. Rust offered a way to build native applications without a VM, IPC, or JavaScript. By using HTML and CSS for the UI and borrowing reactive ideas from React, Dioxus could reuse a great deal of web tooling and web components while remaining familiar to developers.

The premise sounded easy, but competing with React Native and Flutter was highly ambitious. In 2021 there were few off-the-shelf components available for Dioxus. The team had to build reactivity, font rendering, hot reloading, application bundling, and much more from scratch. Even building a web browser became a necessary step along the way.

What five years of infrastructure work produced

By 2026, Kelley says Dioxus has met and exceeded its original mission. It supports cross-platform development, native rendering, Rust hot reload, and bundle splitting. The project has effectively reinvented and improved much of the application-development stack.

Developers can ship a full-stack web application from the same codebase that shares components with iOS and Android applications. The project has nearly 37,000 GitHub stars and millions of downloads, and applications built with Dioxus are used around the world by an estimated 200 million end users. They include AI assistants, voting software, data-science tools, and satellite collision-avoidance systems.

The team has invested heavily in making Dioxus approachable: fewer files, build tooling, hot reload, asset optimization, and the pieces needed to ship on multiple platforms. Because Dioxus applications are written in Rust, their structure is simple and developers rarely need to fall back to platform-specific code. A new project can begin with a main.rs file rather than an elaborate build-system setup.

One especially ambitious effort was Blitz, a lightweight but fully featured HTML and CSS rendering engine. The team extracted Firefox's browser-grade CSS engine, built its own HTML DOM, and developed a hybrid GPU rendering pipeline. Compared with Electron applications, Blitz applications can use bundles below five megabytes and less than 50 megabytes of RAM at runtime. Developers can also build custom components and heavily customize the browser experience.

The team also built Subsecond, a generic hot-reload engine for Rust, C, and C++. It watches for edits, recompiles the changed code, and patches the running application in place in roughly 100 milliseconds. Kelley describes it as an unusually difficult challenge and says it supports a broad range of languages and runtimes across major systems, including the web through WebAssembly.

These projects were the result of a small team closely reviewing its work and maintaining a frequent, ambitious release cadence. Until recently, every line of Dioxus code had been painstakingly written by hand.

Adopting coding agents without becoming a slop cannon

Software development changed dramatically in the previous six months as AI coding agents became much better, particularly at Rust. Kelley says his team, made up of experienced Rust engineers, had been skeptical of AI. They had not been using it day to day because they assumed high-quality code and AI tooling were incompatible.

Seeing agents become effective at Rust changed that. The team expanded its use of coding tools, maximized its Claude Code subscriptions, generated tens of thousands of lines of Rust, and built features it had wanted for a long time. Yet little of that generated work initially cleared the team's bar for merging. Features, fixes, and integrations remained in draft because the team did not yet know how to wield the tools properly. It was too easy to become what Kelley calls a "slop cannon."

The team reflected on what worked and what did not. Dioxus had always aimed to be easy to read and write, with good tools and error messages. Coding agents do not particularly value those qualities on their own. The team had tried to make Rust easier through Dioxus because Rust is difficult to write, but agents now take on much of that development burden: they handle edge cases and fight the borrow checker. The learning curve the team had worked to reduce may now be a feature.

Their adoption process produced lessons about the work agents already do well and the work they are not yet ready to do. Those lessons matter especially for ambitious software projects.

The quality substrate of ambitious software

Kelley distinguishes ambitious software from research code, rapid prototypes, or applications whose users only see the exterior. For Dioxus, the code must work reliably and be easy to fix when it breaks. Teams need to keep building maintainable code because delivery velocity rests on the substrate they have built; if that substrate is weak, nothing built on top of it will be good.

The team also needs to ship features. Its roadmap extends far into the future, with many Dioxus features still to build. The challenge is to move quickly without sacrificing quality, breaking APIs in patch releases, or disrupting the millions of people who rely on the project. For software on which people build businesses, documentation, examples, tests, and benchmarks all have to meet a high bar. Users notice quickly when any of those are out of place.

Coding agents can be excellent assistants for difficult technical problems because they bring patience and broad knowledge that an individual working on a large software project cannot easily match. Many Dioxus problems are knowledge problems: the team cannot know every detail of every build system, runtime, operating system, programming language, API, or implementation quirk.

Where agents make hard work tractable

This breadth of knowledge is where coding agents excel. They can sift through thousands of pages of documentation, read bespoke APIs, inspect binaries, and reverse-engineer interfaces with more patience than an individual developer. Kelley gives the example of Kotlin and Swift plugins deeply integrated into Dioxus's build system. Work comparable to React Native Turbo Modules took years to develop manually, while the team was able to ship its implementation in roughly two to three weeks with coding agents. The implementation itself was completed in about a day; the remaining time went to building test cases and testing on real devices.

Agents also accelerated debugging in Blitz, Dioxus's custom web engine. They can help with difficult CSS, styling, and layout issues because they know the CSS specification well. When a developer is trying to resolve painting or layout behavior, an agent can recall how Chrome and Safari handle it, saving the developer from digging through deeply nested WebKit source repositories.

The result is that the team can invest time in doing things correctly rather than taking shortcuts. In the past, people often judged a project by its complexity and chose shortcuts to ship faster, even if that lowered quality. Coding agents can make it more feasible to preserve quality while taking the proper path.

Using agents for maintenance and release discipline

Less glamorous uses of agents can be especially valuable for ambitious projects. Dioxus has a small core team of three engineers, so time spent verifying that a tarball extracts into the right directory structure is time not spent thinking about architecture and harder problems. Maintaining a high bar over a large codebase and every release is challenging. A release might add an extension for a new editor such as Zed, and the team may not be able to test that editor during every patch release. Such integrations are easy to break.

Applying agents to these problems lets the team automate tedious and difficult tasks that would previously have taken many hours. For Dioxus, the code is the product: people download it, build on it, use its APIs, read its documentation, and depend on its architecture. A lapse in the quality of code or SDKs directly worsens the developer experience, can stall customers' businesses, and can cause users to abandon the product.

Kelley says agents have been excellent at release checklists, backporting bug fixes to stable releases, and helping keep documentation at a high standard. The team still writes many documentation comments itself, but it is easy to assign an agent the task of ensuring that everything is documented correctly and includes examples. Humans may edit code without updating the accompanying comment, leaving confusing stale documentation over time.

The team has shipped more patch releases in its most recent Dioxus version than ever before. It has been able to sustain weekly, and sometimes multiple-times-per-week, releases for a large and ambitious piece of software in a way that would previously have felt too risky.

The limits of AI-written tests and the importance of architecture

Kelley is not yet fully convinced by using AI to write tests blindly. Dioxus has struggled with testing because foundational software and complex systems are difficult to test end to end. It is hard, for example, to prove that an extension installs into Zed and behaves correctly without actually opening Zed and using the extension.

Coding agents struggle with this too. They may write superficial tests, such as testing a constructor merely because it exists. They can write tests for a given API, but, like humans, they often fail to choose the right tests. The team still enumerates test conditions manually, crafts test APIs itself, and handles test runners. Agents can nevertheless be useful sounding boards for generating test ideas and identifying edge conditions that need coverage.

One testing task the team has enjoyed assigning to agents is building test harnesses. Fuzzing is critical for production-grade software: it subjects an application to millions of inputs, often malformed or adversarial inputs and ways users should not use the software but still can. Kelley says coding agents are excellent at building these harnesses.

Code architecture remains an art. Coding agents enable exceptionally high delivery velocity, but if the substrate on which their code lands is poor, their contributions will be poor as well. Unlike human engineers, agents are not usually reluctant to begin a large refactor or redesign when a feature does not fit; they will often simply ship something. Much of the team's development time is therefore now spent on architecture, future features, and how the system will evolve. Agents can write spaghetti code just as people can, only faster.

With capable tools, Kelley believes code quality can be very high when teams communicate intent clearly. As a result, software architecture may occupy most of the work in the future, while the act of writing code takes less time.

Code is cheap; quality is not

At Dioxus, the team still reviews every pull request line by line. It uses AI review to find bugs early, but it also wants to read the code it ships. As a large open-source project, Dioxus receives many pull requests from strangers, and not all of them are equivalent. Contributors can be poor at communicating their intent to models and may not think deeply about how the codebase should evolve. They may only want a particular fix or feature, leaving solutions glued into place.

Coding agents cannot read the team's mind, so development is still constrained by text. Kelley argues that prompt engineering is real: implementation quality can depend heavily on the prompt given to the model. But he also sees continuity with established engineering practice. Reading code has always been more important than writing it, particularly as a project matures.

His closing view is that code is now cheap, but quality is not. The job of a software engineer has never merely been to put lines of code on a screen. It is to design elegant solutions to complex problems, think far ahead about how systems evolve, and retain flexibility as requirements change. Those responsibilities have not changed, and the bar for software engineering is higher than ever.

Kelley closes by noting that Cognition, which acquired Dioxus, is hiring people to work on the next generation of software tools. The Dioxus team joined Cognition to help build that future.
aiSummary: Dioxus 创始人 Jonathan Kelley 分享小型 Rust 框架团队如何借助编码智能体加速跨平台基础设施建设，同时守住架构纪律、测试严谨性、文档与评审标准。
oneSentenceSummary: Dioxus 创始人 Jonathan Kelley 分享小型 Rust 框架团队如何借助编码智能体加速跨平台基础设施建设，同时守住架构纪律、测试严谨性、文档与评审标准。
summary: Jonathan Kelley 回顾了 Dioxus 从 Rust 跨平台构想出发，历经五年发展为具备原生渲染、Web 与移动端共享组件、热重载及自有渲染基础设施的框架。他以 Blitz 和 Subsecond 说明，要让雄心勃勃的开发者工具可靠可用，需要投入大量工程工作。核心观点并非智能体能够取代工程判断：智能体可以承担文档调研、不熟悉 API 的研究、调试、发布检查、回补和测试工具搭建，让小团队将更多精力放在困难的工程决策上。Kelley 也指出这种杠杆的边界：早期生成的功能常达不到项目质量门槛，端到端测试与测试选择仍需人工引导，智能体也能快速产出与现有架构不契合的实现。结论是，实现成本下降并未削弱对可维护基础、明确意图、逐行评审和长期设计的要求，反而提升了这些要求的重要性。

mainPoints.point: 雄心勃勃的框架需要持久可靠的工程底座
mainPoints.explanation: Kelley 将 Dioxus 描述为不只是跨平台 UI 层：原生渲染、工具链、热重载、文档、测试与发布纪律都必须保持可维护，因为下游用户会在框架之上构建自己的业务。

mainPoints.point: 智能体能缩短知识密集型基础设施工作的周期
mainPoints.explanation: 演讲将文档调研、定制 API 调查、构建集成、CSS 调试、发布检查和回补列为智能体特别有价值的任务，让三人团队能把更多时间用于棘手的工程判断。

mainPoints.point: 生成代码需要质量体系，而不是不加辨别地采用
mainPoints.explanation: 团队早期生成了大量未达到合并标准的 Rust 代码。Kelley 认为，可读性、有效的错误信息、明确的评审和测试，才是防止智能体辅助交付滑向低质量产出的约束。

mainPoints.point: 测试与架构仍是人类主导的责任
mainPoints.explanation: 智能体可以搭建有价值的模糊测试和测试工具，但并不总能挑选有意义的端到端测试，也难以预判设计的演进方向。工程师仍须定义条件、权衡取舍并保护架构的灵活性。

keyQuotes: Kelley 认为，变成一门「代码垃圾炮」实在太容易了。
交付速度建立在已打好的工程底座之上；如果这个底座薄弱，其上构建的一切都不会好。
编码智能体能让人在坚持正确路径时更有可能守住质量。
代码如今很便宜，但质量并不便宜。
